01The System

Unified Transaction Across Three Platforms

A single branch transaction traverses up to three different platforms, each operated by distinct personnel.

Utilized by customers

E-form

Initiates the process: customers verify their identity, select the transaction type, and input necessary details.

Utilized by bankers

Tablet

Bankers review customer profiles and transaction data, perform validation, and finalize the transaction.

Utilized by staff and supervisory personnel

Branch Administration

Responsibilities include editing customer profiles, configuring branch parameters, opening and closing branches, and approving transactions.

02Identified Issues

Manual verification relied heavily on visual checking.

Prior to the Smart Branch implementation, customers queued, completed paper forms, and awaited processing. Bankers then manually verified the forms, the individual, and, in the case of corporate clients, the authority of representatives.

Verification Methods

Identity

Visual comparison against ID cards.

Cash Amount

Manually written on paper forms, susceptible to alteration.

Company Authority

Confirmed through telephone verification.

Special Rate

Treasury code retrieved from a secondary system.

Audit Trail

Limited; system did not enforce verification procedures.

04The Objective

Enhance controls without increasing customer wait times.

Aim: Replace paper-based processes with automated, system-validated, end-to-end transaction recording. The challenge involved balancing security measures and processing speed.

Security Enhancements

  • System validation of all customer data, eliminating manual identity checks.
  • Implementation of strict rules with flexible authentication for legitimate exceptions.
  • Timestamping of every transaction.
  • Comprehensive records indicating customer identity, processing banker, approving banker, and validation method.

Efficiency Improvements

  • Streamlined core process: ID input, facial recognition, validation, and continuation.
  • Transaction history storage to facilitate repeat transactions.
  • Support for combining multiple transactions within a single session.

Case study

Product Designer · Nov 2021 – Apr 2022

Online learning platform in Indonesia

Results measured from Nov 2021 to Apr 2022.

Design Strategy

The challenge

Enrollment was initiated on WhatsApp, causing friction between discovering a program and enrolling.

The approach

Instead of merely replicating WhatsApp steps online, I redesigned the user journey around program discovery, evaluation, and registration.

  1. Previously

    Enrollment used a manual WhatsApp chat, separate from where users found the program.

  2. New plan

    Focused on discovery, evaluation, and enrollment, rather than old chat steps.

  3. Outcome

    Consolidated home, program list, detail, and enrollment in a single website flow.

  4. Impact

    57% higher onboarding rate, with all enrollments now via the website.

My contributions

Led the overhaul of the platform, including the Courses Marketplace, Student Dashboard, and CMS Admin.

  • Introduced the website enrollment process to replace the manual WhatsApp system.
  • Crafted the Courses Marketplace to facilitate program discovery and user onboarding.
  • Designed an analytical CMS to monitor program performance and guide decision-making.
  • Participated in PRD development and conducted UAT to ensure feature validation.

Smart Branch · Featured Deep Dive: Verification of Cash Transactions

Ensuring Accountability in Cash Operations

Transactions involving cash deposits, withdrawals, and foreign currency exchanges at special rates for individual clients and corporate representatives.

Role
Product Designer
Features
01 and 02
Clients
Individuals and Corporate Representatives
Platforms
E-form, Tablet, Branch Management System

Historical Challenges

Within the branch, each cash transaction was dependent on a banker manually verifying all details. Customers queued, completed paper forms, waited to be called, and only then were the forms, the individuals, and, in the case of corporate clients, the representatives’ authority checked manually. For corporate withdrawals, the banker also contacted the company to confirm the transaction. For special rate transactions, the banker referenced the treasury code in a secondary system.

The system did not safeguard these procedures. There was no restriction preventing unauthorized persons from executing company transactions, and deposit or withdrawal form amounts could be altered after submission.

The constraint was that banking procedures mandated a maker and an approver. This requirement had to be integrated into the system, with records that were tamper-proof, without introducing delays for the customer.

My Contribution: Quantifying Cash within the System

Initially, I proposed a consent checkbox. This was replaced with a screen where the banker inputs the counted amount, which is then matched against the amount entered by the customer on the e-form. If discrepancies are found, the transaction cannot proceed.

Option A

Consent checkbox only

The banker checks a box to confirm the correctness of the amount. This approach is swift but provides no record of the counting process; the banker’s assertion stands as the only proof.

Option B

Count and match (preferred)

The banker recounts cash by denomination within the system. The total must match the e-form amount before proceeding, and the counting is recorded with a timestamp.

This process is symmetric: for deposits, the banker counts the received cash; for withdrawals, the counted cash is the amount handed over. Additionally, a denomination calculator was integrated, considering bankers already use physical calculators for counting, thereby consolidating the process.

Workflow Overview

For Individual Customers

Completion of the e-form (including ID number, ID photo, face recognition, transaction details, confirmation, and a queue ticket via email), followed by verification and cash counting on the tablet, culminating in system posting and receipt issuance.

For Corporate Representatives

Similar steps with additional company selection; a supervisor reviews the transaction and company details, confirms over WhatsApp, then proceeds with the tablet process.

For Special Rate Transactions

The customer contacts the treasury team to obtain a treasury code. The e-form verifies the name, amount, treasury code, and date; the special rate applies only if all matching conditions are met.

Above banker limit

Transactions exceeding the banker’s limit require supervisor authentication to complete.
